title: How animals learn: getting used to things, linking things, and teaching

summary.text: A sparrow who flies away from a new scarecrow on Monday may be sitting on the scarecrow's head by Friday. She has not become careless. She has learned that the scarecrow does no harm. In the Spoon Test, you check the same thing on two volunteers with a spoon and a plate. You find that getting used to a harmless sound is a kind of learning: it grows with repeats, it is kept, and it belongs to that one sound. Then you look at other kinds of learning. Animals can link a taste to feeling ill after just one time. Bees learn which flowers have nectar, and at what time of day. Meerkats and ants teach. A sea slug with only 20,000 nerve cells learns, and scientists argue about whether a slime mould, with no nerve cells at all, shows a change like learning too. Inside a nervous system, learning is a change in the connections between nerve cells.
summary.art: A sparrow sitting on the clay-pot head of a scarecrow in a rice field, with small pictures around it: a sea slug, a bee at a blue flower, a meerkat helper with a pup, and two nerve cells joined by a tiny gap.

intro.hook: Stop and listen for ten seconds. Is a fan whirring, a fridge humming or a clock ticking? Ten minutes ago, you were not hearing it. Where did the sound go?
intro.text: The sound never stopped. Your mind learned that it does not matter, and left it out. Scientists call this habituation, and it is the simplest kind of learning. In this unit you test it on volunteers with a spoon and a plate. Then you look at how other living things learn: bees, meerkats and songbirds, a sea slug with only 20,000 nerve cells, and a slime mould with no nerve cells at all.
intro.art: A child sitting very still in a living room with a ceiling fan, a fridge and a wall clock, each with faint sound waves that the child has stopped noticing.

outcomes: I can say what learning is, and tell it apart from instinct, growing up and tiredness.
I can describe habituation and show with a test that it is learned: it grows with repeats, and a new sound brings the response back.
I can explain how animals link things that go together, and why some links form in one go.
I can give examples of learning in animals with very small brains, and with none.
I can explain why practice spread over time lasts longer than cramming.
I can tell showing from teaching, and give a real example of an animal that teaches.
I can say in simple words what changes inside a nervous system when something is learned.

terms.meaning: A lasting change in what a living being does, caused by experience.
terms.example: A sparrow stops fleeing a scarecrow that never moves.
terms.art: A sparrow sitting on a scarecrow's hat.

terms.meaning: Anything a living being senses that can make them react, such as a sound, a touch or a smell.
terms.example: The ring of a spoon on a plate is a stimulus.
terms.art: A spoon ringing on a steel plate, with sound lines.

terms.meaning: What a living being does when they sense a stimulus.
terms.example: A person jumps when a spoon rings behind them.
terms.art: A person at a table jumping slightly at a sound from behind.

terms.meaning: A quick response that is ready at birth and does not need to be learned.
terms.example: Blinking when something comes near your eye.
terms.art: A child's eye closing as a cotton ball is tossed near.

terms.meaning: A lasting drop in how strongly a being reacts to something that keeps happening and does no harm.
terms.example: You stop hearing the fridge hum after a while.
terms.art: A person reading calmly while a fridge hums in the background.

terms.meaning: When a new stimulus brings back a response that had grown weak.
terms.example: After ignoring a spoon, a person jumps at a rattling tin.
terms.art: A person jumping at a rattling tin after ignoring a spoon sound.

terms.meaning: A rise in how strongly a being reacts, after a strong or scary event.
terms.example: After thunder, a dog jumps at small sounds.
terms.art: A dog with raised ears under a stormy sky.

terms.meaning: Learning that two things go together, so that one makes you expect the other.
terms.example: A bee links a blue flower with nectar.
terms.art: A bee at a blue flower with a drop of nectar.

terms.meaning: The tiny gap where one nerve cell passes a chemical message to the next.
terms.example: A touch on the skin sets off messages across many synapses.
terms.art: Two nerve cells with a tiny gap between them and chemical dots crossing it.

terms.meaning: Practice spread over time, with breaks between the sittings.
terms.example: Learning a poem in four short sittings through the day.
terms.art: A clock face with four small study sessions marked around it.

terms.meaning: When one animal changes what she does, at a cost to herself, so that another learns faster.
terms.example: A meerkat helper gives a pup a scorpion with the stinger removed.
terms.art: A meerkat helper handing a small crippled scorpion to a pup.

terms.meaning: A change that is kept from an experience, so that it can shape what a being does later.
terms.example: A bee returning at the hour that food was last there.
terms.art: A bee at a window with a clock showing four o'clock.

explanations.definition: Learning is a change in what a living being does, caused by experience, that lasts for some time.
explanations.description: Learning is not instinct, which is ready on the day of birth. It is not growing up, as when a chick's legs get strong. It is not tiredness, because a tired muscle recovers after a rest, while learned changes can stay for days or years. Scientists test for learning by changing a being's experience, and then seeing what she does later.
examples: A sparrow stops fleeing from a scarecrow that never moves.
A bee comes back to the colour of flower that had nectar.
A young songbird sings the song she heard from adults.
explanations.art: A sparrow, a bee and a young songbird, each with a thought bubble showing what they have learned.

explanations.definition: Habituation is a lasting drop in how strongly a being reacts to something that keeps happening and does no harm.
explanations.description: It is the simplest kind of learning. A sea slug pulls in the gill less and less if the same gentle touch is repeated. A person jumps less and less at the same ring of a spoon. Habituation saves energy and attention for what matters. It is also specific to what was repeated. A new sound can bring the full reaction back at once, which is why a sparrow ignores a scarecrow but not a hawk.
examples: You stop hearing the fan in your room.
A sparrow sits on a scarecrow that never moves.
A sea slug stops pulling in the gill when touched gently again and again.
explanations.art: A line of ten spoon rings with the jump of a person drawn smaller each time.

explanations.concept: Learned, or just tired? How scientists tell
explanations.definition: A drop in response counts as habituation, and not as tiredness, when it grows with repeats, when a new stimulus still gets a full response, and when the drop is only for the stimulus that was repeated.
explanations.description: In 1966, Richard Thompson and William Spencer listed the signs that a drop in response is learned and not tiredness. First, the response gets smaller with each repeat. Second, a rest lets it come back a little. Third, a different stimulus still gets a full reaction, because the drop belongs to the old stimulus only. A tired being would react less to everything, so a strong response to a new sound shows that only the old sound has been learned as harmless. A strong new stimulus can also bring back the reaction to the old one, and that is called dishabituation. Sounds that are weaker or that come faster are usually ignored sooner.
examples: After ignoring a spoon, a person jumps at a rattling tin.
A sea slug that ignores a gentle touch still pulls in the gill at a stronger touch.
A person who stopped hearing the fridge hears it again when it stops.
explanations.art: Two graphs side by side: tiredness falling for all sounds, and habituation falling for one sound with a spike for a new one.

explanations.definition: Sensitisation is a rise in how strongly a being reacts to many things, after a strong or scary event.
explanations.description: A sea slug given a sharp shock to the tail pulls in the gill more strongly, even at a gentle touch, for a while. A dog who has heard thunder jumps at small sounds afterwards. Habituation turns a response down for one harmless thing. Sensitisation turns the alertness up for everything. Together they let a being set how watchful to be.
examples: A dog is jumpy after fireworks.
A sea slug pulls in the gill harder after a shock to the tail.
You jump at the next creak after a scary film.
explanations.art: A sea slug with a strong gill pull after a tail shock, beside one with a weak pull after gentle touches.

explanations.definition: Association is learning that two things go together, so that one makes the being expect the other.
explanations.description: In the early 1900s, Ivan Pavlov showed that a bell that came before food made dogs drool at the bell alone. Bees link a flower colour with nectar. Some links form fast. After one bad meal, a person or animal may avoid that taste for years. In 1966, John Garcia and Robert Koelling found that rats link a taste with feeling ill, even when the illness comes a long time later. Rats do not link a flash of light or a click with feeling ill. A body is ready for some links more than for others, and the ready ones are often the ones that keep a being alive.
examples: A cat comes running at the sound of a tin being opened.
A child avoids a food that once made her ill.
A bee returns to blue flowers that gave nectar.
explanations.art: A rat with a taste cup and a flashing light, linked by an arrow to feeling ill only from the taste cup.

explanations.definition: Honeybees and bumblebees learn the colour, smell, shape and place of flowers that have nectar, and even the time of day.
explanations.description: A honeybee's brain has about a million nerve cells, and a human brain has about 86 billion. Yet bees learn a lot. In 1929, Ingeborg Beling showed that honeybees fed at the same time each day came at that time on later days, even with no food there. In 2017, Olli Loukola, Lars Chittka and colleagues showed that bumblebees can learn to roll a ball to a goal for sugar by watching another bee, while bees that saw no demonstration learned more slowly. So learning does not need a big brain. It needs a body that can change with experience.
examples: A honeybee returns to a feeder at four o'clock each day.
A bumblebee learns to roll a ball by watching another bee.
A bee switches to a new flower colour when the old one stops giving nectar.
explanations.art: A bumblebee rolling a small ball towards a circle marked with sugar, while another bee watches.

explanations.description: A bacterium swimming towards food compares how much food there is now with how much there was a few seconds ago, which is a tiny memory (Segall, Block and Berg, 1986). Stentor, a trumpet-shaped one-celled animal in ponds, first bends away from a puff of particles, and after many puffs stops reacting (Herbert Spencer Jennings, 1906, confirmed by Donald Wood in the 1970s). In 2016, Audrey Dussutour and colleagues showed that slime moulds, which are single giant cells, at first avoided a harmless bitter bridge on the way to food, and after several days got used to crossing it. In 2014, Monica Gagliano and colleagues reported that the plant Mimosa pudica, the touch-me-not, stopped folding the leaves when dropped again and again, and still ignored the drop about a month later. Scientists agree that these changes happen. They argue about whether to call them learning.
examples: A slime mould crosses a bitter bridge that was first avoided.
A touch-me-not plant stops folding the leaves at a harmless drop.
Stentor stops contracting after many puffs of particles.

perspectives.who: Scientists who link learning to nervous systems
perspectives.explanation: Learning needs nerve cells that change their connections. In a one-celled animal or a plant, the change may be the cell's chemistry simply adjusting, and a different word would be clearer.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study simple living things
perspectives.explanation: If a change is kept, grows with repeats and belongs to one stimulus, it passes the same tests as habituation in a sea slug. Nerve cells are one way to learn, but not the only way.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists who ask for more tests
perspectives.explanation: The Mimosa result is striking. Other laboratories want to repeat it, and to make sure that the cells that move the leaf were not simply tired.

explanations.art: A slime mould spreading over a bridge of oats, a trumpet-shaped Stentor in pond water, and a touch-me-not plant with open leaves.

explanations.concept: Where the learning is kept: connections between nerve cells
explanations.definition: A synapse is the tiny gap where one nerve cell passes a chemical message to the next, and learning changes how strongly synapses pass the message.
explanations.description: In a sea slug, repeated gentle touches make the touch-sensing cell release less chemical across its synapse, so the gill pulls in less. A shock makes it release more. In 1949, Donald Hebb suggested that when one cell repeatedly helps to fire the next, the connection between them grows stronger. The phrase 'cells that fire together wire together' is often credited to Carla Shatz (1992). In people, Eleanor Maguire and colleagues found in 2000 that London taxi drivers, who learn about 25,000 streets, had a larger back part of the hippocampus, a part of the brain used for places. In 2011, trainee taxi drivers who passed their exam were found to have grown that part, and trainees who failed had not. So learning leaves a physical mark.
examples: A sea slug's touch-sensing cell sends less chemical after many touches.
A taxi driver's hippocampus grows as they learn the streets.
A path in grass gets clearer each time someone walks on it. In the same way, a connection between nerve cells gets stronger with use.
explanations.art: Two nerve cells with a gap between them, with fewer chemical dots crossing on one side and more on the other.

explanations.definition: Many young songbirds learn their songs by hearing adults of their own kind during a window in early life.
explanations.description: A young male zebra finch copies the song of his father. Peter Marler's experiments in the 1960s and 1970s showed that a young white-crowned sparrow raised alone sang only a rough, simple song. A young bird that hears adults in the right weeks first makes soft, messy sounds, and then practises until his song is fixed. Birds of the same kind in different places sing slightly different dialects. So a song is partly born in the bird and partly learned from the group.
examples: A young male zebra finch copies his father's song.
White-crowned sparrows in different places sing different dialects.
A young white-crowned sparrow raised alone sings a rough song.
explanations.art: A young bird listening to an adult bird sing, with notes drifting between them.

explanations.description: In 1992, Tim Caro and Marc Hauser said that animal teaching needs three things. The teacher changes what she does only when a learner is near. It costs her something. And the learner learns faster. In 2006, Alex Thornton and Katherine McAuliffe showed that meerkat helpers give young pups dead scorpions, and give live ones as the pups get older. In 2006, Nigel Franks and Tom Richardson studied tandem runs, where one ant leads another. They showed that the leader ant slows down and waits when the follower falls behind, which costs her time. Scientists agree on what these animals do. They argue about whether to call it teaching.
examples: A meerkat helper gives a pup a scorpion with the stinger removed.
A leader ant waits for a follower in a tandem run.
A person slows down to show a child a fold.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use the three tests
perspectives.explanation: The helper and the ant pass all three tests. The animal changes what she does, the change costs her something, and the learner learns faster. That is teaching, whatever the animal is thinking.
In people, a teacher knows what the learner does not know. We cannot tell whether a meerkat or an ant knows this, so some scientists prefer to call it 'helping to learn'.

explanations.art: A meerkat helper offering a crippled scorpion to a pup, and a leader ant waiting for a follower who is touching her back.

explanations.definition: Spaced practice is practice spread over time with breaks, and it usually leaves a longer-lasting memory than the same practice done all at once.
explanations.description: In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus reported that learning spread over several days beat the same learning crammed together. Sea slugs show it too. In 1972, Thomas Carew, Harold Pinsker and Eric Kandel found that when touches were spread over days, a sea slug stayed used to the touch for weeks. The same number of touches in one block did not last as long. Randolf Menzel and colleagues found a similar result in honeybees in 2001. A cell needs time to build new parts for a lasting memory, and the breaks between sittings give it that time.
examples: Four short sittings through a day beat one long sitting for a list of words.
Touches spread over days make a longer-lasting change in a sea slug.
Honeybees remember a flower better after spaced visits.
explanations.art: Two bars on a graph: a short bar labelled all at once and a tall bar labelled spread out, with a sea slug beside them.

agreed.text: Habituation is found in almost every kind of animal that has been tested, from sea slugs to humans.
agreed.evidence: Richard Thompson and William Spencer (1966) listed the same signs in many species, and later work added more.

agreed.text: Learning changes the connections between nerve cells.
agreed.evidence: Eric Kandel's team (from 1970) found that when a sea slug gets used to a touch, less chemical crosses one synapse.

agreed.text: Practice spread over time usually lasts longer than practice crammed together.
agreed.evidence: It has been found in people, in honeybees (Menzel and colleagues, 2001) and in sea slugs (Carew, Pinsker and Kandel, 1972).

agreed.text: Animals are ready to link some things more easily than others.
agreed.evidence: John Garcia and Robert Koelling (1966) found that rats link a taste with feeling ill, but not a light or a click.

agreed.text: Many young songbirds need to hear adults of their own kind in order to sing the right song.
agreed.evidence: Peter Marler's experiments with white-crowned sparrows raised alone, in the 1960s and 1970s.

agreed.text: Bees learn the colours, smells and times of day of rewarding flowers.
agreed.evidence: Ingeborg Beling (1929) showed time learning, and many studies since have shown colour and scent learning.

challenging.claim: Slime moulds and one-celled animals learn.
challenging.for: Slime moulds and Stentor show a drop in response that is kept and belongs to one stimulus, as in sea slugs.
challenging.against: Some scientists say learning needs nerve cells, and that these are simpler changes in the cell's chemistry.

challenging.claim: Plants such as the touch-me-not learn.
challenging.for: Plants dropped many times stopped folding the leaves, and still ignored the drop about a month later.
challenging.against: Other laboratories want to repeat the result, and to make sure the leaf cells were not simply tired.

challenging.claim: Some animals, such as meerkats and ants, teach.
challenging.who: Alex Thornton, Nigel Franks and others
challenging.for: The animals change what they do, at a cost, and the learners learn faster.
challenging.against: We cannot tell whether the teachers know what the learner does not know.

challenging.claim: A memory sits in a particular group of cells, called an engram.
challenging.who: Susumu Tonegawa, Sheena Josselyn and others
challenging.for: In mice, switching on a set of cells that were active during an event can bring back the memory of that event.
challenging.against: Other results suggest that memories are spread across many cells and can shift over time.

big_questions.q: A sparrow ignores a scarecrow but flies from a hawk. Is she paying less attention, or is she better at noticing what matters?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Spoon Test. The person ignored the spoon but jumped at the rice tin.

big_questions.q: A slime mould has no nerve cells, yet gets used to a bitter bridge. Does learning need a mind?
big_questions.hint: What do you think learning is: a change that is kept, or something that needs a brain?

big_questions.q: Is a memory kept in one place, or is it a way that many cells are connected?
big_questions.hint: Karl Lashley cut away parts of rats' brains and never found one spot where a memory lived. Eric Kandel traced a simple memory in a sea slug to a single connection between cells.

big_questions.q: A person gets sick once from a food, and avoids it for years. Is that learning too fast, or learning well?
big_questions.hint: In nature, a food that once made you ill may do it again.

big_questions.q: If a being gets used to everything harmless, what is left for her to notice?
big_questions.hint: In the story The Hat on the Scarecrow, the sparrows ignored the scarecrow but noticed the hawk. What kinds of things are worth noticing?

big_questions.q: What do you ignore every day, and who or what taught you to ignore it?
big_questions.hint: Think of noises, smells, signs, and other people's troubles.

big_questions.q: Do animals who teach their young know what they are doing?
big_questions.hint: A meerkat helper gives a pup an easier scorpion first. Does she need to understand this to do it?

story.title: The Hat on the Scarecrow
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Birds get used to a scarecrow that never changes or does anything, and farmers keep a scarer working by changing it and moving it. The village, the people and the die plan are imagined.
text: Kavya was nine, and every January she stayed with her Thatha, her grandfather, in a village near Thanjavur. The week before Pongal, the rice in his field turned gold and heavy. That was the week the sparrows and munias came to eat it.

Thatha had a scarecrow for them. Its head was an old black clay pot with a white face painted on it. Its body was a bamboo cross, dressed in one of Thatha's torn white shirts, and a red towel flapped from one arm. Thatha called him Mani.

On Monday, when the birds came, they stopped in the air. They circled and chirped. Then they settled on the far side of the road, thirty steps from Mani. Thatha folded his arms. 'Birds are not clever,' he said. 'Show them a face, and they run.'
Kavya had a new notebook, and her teacher had told her to write what she saw, not what she expected. So she sat on the bund, the low mud wall of the field, and watched.

On Tuesday, the birds sat on the fence, twenty steps from Mani. On Wednesday, they sat ten steps away. On Thursday, three munias walked along the bund right beside his feet and pecked at the grain. Kavya wrote it all down. On Friday morning, a sparrow flew up and landed on the clay pot. She put her head on one side and sat there, looking at the field.
'Foolish bird!' shouted Thatha. He threw a clod of earth, and the sparrow flew off. In a minute, she was back on the pot.

'Thatha,' said Kavya, 'she is not foolish. Look at my notebook.' She showed him the steps: thirty, twenty, ten, none. 'On Monday, Mani was new. The birds did not know what he was. But every day he stood there, and every day nothing happened. He never moved. He never shouted. He never hurt anyone. So they learned that he is harmless.'
'Learned?' said Thatha. 'A sparrow?'
'She learned to ignore him,' said Kavya. 'That is a kind of learning. My teacher says even a sea slug gets used to a touch that never hurts.'
Thatha was quiet for a while. Then he laughed. 'So my clever scarecrow has taught the birds to ignore scarecrows.'
'Yes,' said Kavya. She laughed too.
'Then what do I do, learned one?' asked Thatha. He was not joking. He wanted to know.
Kavya thought hard. 'Birds get used to what stays the same,' she said. 'So we must not let Mani stay the same.'

That evening, she made a plan. Every morning, they would move Mani to a different corner of the field. They would tie a steel plate to a long string, and a spoon beside it, so that pulling the string made a loud ting across the field. But if they rang it at the same hour every day, the birds would learn that too. So Kavya took the die from her snakes and ladders box. Every half hour, she would roll it. On a six, she would pull the string. On a one, she would tie the red towel to the other arm.
'A dice game guarding my rice,' said Thatha, shaking his head. But he moved Mani.
On Saturday, the birds kept far away. On Sunday, too. Kavya's notebook said: no birds closer than thirty steps, all day.

On Sunday afternoon, something happened that Kavya did not plan. She and Thatha were sitting under the neem tree, and nobody had touched the string. Suddenly every sparrow and munia on the bund burst into the air at once, without a single chirp. They dropped into the thick rice and vanished.
A moment later, a small grey hawk slid low across the field from the coconut palms. She turned her head one way, then the other. She found nothing, and she flew on.
Thatha had stopped breathing. 'They did not even look at Mani,' he whispered, 'but they saw her before I did.'
Kavya was already writing. 'They stopped looking at the things that do not matter,' she said slowly. 'So they could keep looking at the things that do.'
On Kaanum Pongal, the day for feeding the birds, Kavya put cooked rice on a banana leaf at the edge of the field. The sparrows came and ate beside Mani's feet. One of them sat on the clay pot again.
Thatha raised his hand, and Kavya thought he would shoo her away. Instead, he lowered it. 'Let her sit,' he said. 'She has earned it.'
story.epiphany: The sparrows had not stopped paying attention. They had learned that a thing that never changes and never hurts does not matter, so they could save their attention for a real danger.
ask: Why did the sparrows stop being afraid of a scarecrow that stood still every day?
The sparrows ignored the scarecrow, but they still flew up when a hawk came. What does that tell you about getting used to something?
How could a farmer keep a scarecrow working for more than a few days?

games.title: Bee School: which flower pays?
games.context: In this guessing game, one player is the garden keeper and the others are bees. The bees must work out which flower colour gives nectar. The keeper changes the colour during the game without telling them, so the bees learn only from whether they get nectar.

setup.art: Three flower cards, blue, yellow and red, laid in a row on a table, with three face-down cards in front of the garden keeper.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three flower cards. The garden keeper shuffles the three rule cards face down.

setup.art: A bee player sliding a finger onto the blue flower card while the garden keeper looks at a hidden rule card.
setup.caption: 2. Each round, every bee picks a flower. The keeper says nectar or nothing.

setup.art: A score sheet with three blocks of eight boxes, with some boxes circled for nectar.
setup.caption: 3. Write your picks in the score sheet. Circle every nectar.

printables.title: 3 flower cards: blue, yellow and red
3 rule cards for the garden keeper

items.b: Blue pays. Yellow and red give nothing.
Yellow pays. Blue and red give nothing.
Red pays. Blue and yellow give nothing.

printables.title: 3 score blocks, one for every 8 rounds
items: Block 1, rounds 1 to 8. Draw eight boxes. In each box write B, Y or R. Circle the box if you got nectar.
Block 2, rounds 9 to 16. Draw eight boxes. In each box write B, Y or R. Circle the box if you got nectar.
Block 3, rounds 17 to 24. Draw eight boxes. In each box write B, Y or R. Circle the box if you got nectar.

rules: One player is the garden keeper. The other players are bees. With two players, swap roles for a second game. With one child, the parent is the garden keeper. Bees write their pick on their own sheet before the keeper says 'nectar', so they cannot copy each other.

The keeper shuffles the three rule cards and lays them face down in a row. Nobody looks at them. The first card is the rule for rounds 1 to 8. The second is for rounds 9 to 16. The third is for rounds 17 to 24.
Each round, every bee writes B, Y or R on their own score sheet to pick blue, yellow or red. The keeper looks at the rule for that block.
The keeper says 'nectar' to each bee who picked the paying colour, and says nothing to each bee who did not. Bees circle their box if they got nectar.
The keeper must never say which colour pays, and never says when the rule changes.
After round 24, each bee counts the nectar in each block. The bee with the most nectar in total wins. If there is a tie, the tied bees share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the flower cards and the rule cards. Choose the garden keeper. Shuffle the rule cards and lay them face down. Each bee draws a score sheet with three blocks of eight boxes.
flow.say: One of us is the garden keeper. The others are bees. The bees must find out which flower has nectar. The keeper will change the paying flower, and will not say when.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Pick a garden keeper. Draw your score sheet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bee School. You set up the cards and the score sheets.

flow.do: Play rounds 1 to 8. Each bee writes a colour. The keeper says 'nectar' to each bee who picked the paying colour, and says nothing to the others. Bees circle the box if they got nectar.
flow.say: Round one. Pick a flower. Write it down. Now I will say 'nectar' if you got some. If I say nothing, you got none. Round two. Pick again.
flow.kid: Play rounds 1 to 8. Pick a colour. Circle it if you got nectar.

ask.q: After a few rounds, which flower are you picking, and why?
good: The one that gave me nectar.
The blue one, because it paid twice.
I am still trying all three.

flow.context: In this step you play the first eight rounds and find the paying flower.

flow.do: Play rounds 9 to 16. The keeper turns to the second rule card without saying anything. Watch how long the bees take to switch.
flow.say: Keep going. Pick a flower each round. Remember that I do not say if anything has changed.
flow.kid: Play rounds 9 to 16. Keep picking. The paying flower may have changed.

ask.q: What happened to your nectar when the rule changed? What did you do next?
good: I got nothing for a few rounds.
I kept picking the old flower for too long.
I tried the other flowers until one paid.

check.q: A bee keeps picking the old paying flower after the rule changes. What is she doing?
options: Using something she learned, even though it has stopped being true
check.why: A bee keeps using a link she has learned, even after it has stopped being true. Real bees do this too. It takes some rounds of getting nothing before she learns the new link. Nobody is silly. Learning always has this delay.

flow.context: In this step you play rounds 9 to 16, when the paying flower has changed.

flow.do: Play rounds 17 to 24 with the third rule card. Keep writing and circling.
flow.say: Last block. The garden has changed once more. Pick your flowers.
flow.kid: Play the last eight rounds. Keep writing and circling.
flow.context: In this step you play the last eight rounds.

flow.do: Each bee counts the nectar in each block, and in total. Say who won. Talk about the rounds just after each change.
flow.say: How much nectar did you get in each block? Which block was your lowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count your nectar in each block. Which block had the least? Why?
flow.think: Why did the nectar drop in the middle of the game?
flow.context: This is the last step of Bee School. You count the nectar and look back.

experiments.title: The Spoon Test: does a person get used to a sound that keeps being harmless?
experiments.question: If a steel spoon rings on a plate again and again behind someone, do their jumps get smaller? If they do, is the person only tired, or have they learned something?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the jumps get smaller, stay the same or get bigger? Then guess what a brand new sound will do. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same plate, the same spoon and the same ring every time. Stand one arm's length behind the volunteer, and wait the same 15 seconds between sounds. Each volunteer does the same puzzle and sits in the same way. Score every sound with the same card, straight away. When you shake the rice tin, only the sound changes, so any change in the jump comes from the sound being new.

materials.item: a steel plate (thali) and a steel spoon
a small steel tin or dabba with a handful of dry rice inside, closed tightly, or a cycle bell
a puzzle, a colouring page or a book for each volunteer
a phone or clock that shows seconds
two willing volunteers, for example a parent and a grandparent
paper and a pencil for the scoring card and the results table

experiments.safety: Ask each volunteer first. Keep the sound at a normal indoor loudness, and never ring it close to an ear. Do not use this test on a baby, on anyone who dislikes sudden sounds, or on anyone with a heart problem. Stop at once if anyone is upset.
experiments.record: For every sound, write a score of 0, 1 or 2 for each volunteer. Then draw one line graph for each volunteer, with the sound number along the bottom and the score up the side. Mark the place where the rice tin came.
experiments.context: In this experiment you ring a spoon on a plate behind two volunteers, again and again, and score how much they jump. You find out whether getting used to a sound is learning.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for one volunteer

setup.art: A paper scoring card with three lines: 0 means no movement, 1 means a small shoulder twitch, 2 means a clear jump or a head turn.
setup.caption: 1. Make a scoring card: 0 is no movement, 1 is a small shoulder twitch, 2 is a jump.

setup.art: A volunteer sitting at a table facing away, doing a colouring page, while a child stands one arm's length behind with a steel plate and spoon.
setup.caption: 2. The volunteer does a puzzle. You stand one arm's length behind.

setup.art: A child ringing the spoon on the plate while looking at a phone clock, with a results table on a clipboard.
setup.caption: 3. Ring the spoon once every 15 seconds. Score each ring at once.

setup.art: After the twelfth ring, the child shakes a small steel tin of rice, and the volunteer's shoulders jump.
setup.caption: 4. After ring 12, shake the rice tin once. Score the jump.

setup.art: A line graph on paper with sound number across and score going up, a dip in the middle, and a spike where the rice tin sound is marked.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a line graph of the scores. Mark the new sound.

flow.do: Show your child the plate, the spoon and the rice tin. Ask two family members if they agree to be volunteers. Write down your child's guesses and reasons.
flow.say: We will ring a spoon on a plate behind someone, again and again. What will their jumps do? Why do you think so? What will a new sound do?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will the jumps get smaller, stay the same or get bigger? Why?

ask.q: What will the jumps do, and why do you think so?
good: They get smaller, because the person learns it is only a spoon.
They stay the same, because a sudden sound always makes you jump.
They get bigger, because the person gets more nervous.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write each guess and its reason at the top of the results table. Ask each volunteer for permission, and tell them that sounds will come from behind them now and then.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spoon Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Make a scoring card with three lines. Score 0 means no movement. Score 1 means a small shoulder twitch or head tilt. Score 2 means a clear jump or a turn of the head.
flow.say: We must agree how to score before we start. Zero is no movement. One is a small shoulder twitch or head tilt. Two is a clear jump or a head turn.
flow.kid: Make a scoring card. Zero is no move. One is a twitch. Two is a jump.
flow.parent: The ringer stands behind, so score only what you can see from behind: shoulders and head. With 2 to 4 children, one rings and one sits to the side and scores; swap roles for the second volunteer, and compare scorers at the end. Decide the three scores now, so that you do not change the rule halfway.

check.q: Why do we agree on the scoring card before the first ring?
options: So every sound is scored by the same rule
So the volunteer knows the answers
check.why: If the rule changed halfway, a smaller score might come from a changed rule, not from a smaller jump. A fixed card keeps the test fair.

flow.context: In this step you make the scoring card, so that every sound is scored the same way.

flow.do: Seat the first volunteer with a puzzle, facing away from you. Stand one arm's length behind. Wait 30 seconds. Then ring the spoon on the plate once every 15 seconds, 12 times. Score each ring.
flow.say: Please do your puzzle and ignore me. A sound will come now and then. Do not try to stop yourself from jumping.
flow.kid: Stand behind the volunteer. Ring the spoon once every 15 seconds. Ring 12 times. Score each one.

ask.q: Are the jumps getting bigger, smaller, or staying the same?
good: They are getting smaller.
They are smaller than at the start.
The last ones are hardly there.

flow.parent: Ring the spoon the same way every time, about a hand-width above the plate, so that each ring is equally loud. Write each score at once. Adults who know a sound is coming may hardly jump at all, even at ring 1. If the first three rings all score 0, ring harder (hit a steel lid or the plate base with the spoon, still at normal indoor loudness) or use a child volunteer, and write down what you changed. If the volunteer tenses up before each ring, make the gaps uneven, between 10 and 20 seconds, and say so in the table.
flow.context: In this step you ring the spoon 12 times behind the first volunteer and score each jump.

flow.do: Straight after ring 12, shake the rice tin once. Score the jump. Then ring the spoon once more, and score that too.
flow.say: Now a different sound. Watch closely. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Shake the rice tin once. Score the jump. Then ring the spoon again. Score it.

ask.q: What did the new sound do, and why do you think so?
good: The jump came back, because the sound was new.
The person noticed it more, because it was different.
The spoon jump stayed small, because the person knew that sound.

check.q: The jump came back for the rice tin. What does this tell us?
options: The person was not simply too tired to react
The rice tin is always louder than the spoon
The person decided to stop jumping at the spoon
check.why: A tired person would jump less at everything. This person jumped again at a new sound, so only the spoon sound had been learned as harmless. If your volunteer jumped less at the tin too, write that down. It means they may be tired, or that the tin sounded like the spoon.

flow.context: In this step you try a new sound after the spoon, to see whether the person is only tired.

flow.do: Let the volunteer chat or drink water for four minutes. Do not mention the sounds. Then ring the spoon three more times, 15 seconds apart. Score each ring.
flow.say: Have a drink and a chat. We will do three more rings in a few minutes.
flow.kid: Let them rest for four minutes. Then ring the spoon three more times. Score each one.
flow.think: After a rest, did the old spoon sound make them jump more, less, or the same?
flow.parent: After a rest the jumps often come back a little. That is normal, and it is part of the pattern. Write exactly what you see.
flow.context: In this step the volunteer rests, and then you try the spoon sound again.

flow.do: Repeat the 12 spoon rings, the rice tin and the rest with the second volunteer. Use the same plate, the same spoon and the same gaps. Score in the second column of the table.
flow.say: Now the second volunteer. We do everything exactly the same, so that we can compare the two.
flow.kid: Do the same with the second volunteer. Use the second column.
flow.parent: If you only have one volunteer, do a second round another day and compare the two days. The answer may differ between people, and that is a result too.
flow.context: In this step you repeat the whole test with a second volunteer.

flow.do: Draw a line graph for each volunteer, with the sound number along the bottom and the score up the side. Mark where the rice tin came. Ask your child to say what they think happened, what they saw in the scores, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think happened? What did you see in the scores? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each volunteer. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.think: If the person were only tired, would a new sound make them jump?
flow.parent: A common pattern is that the jumps got smaller over the 12 spoon sounds, came back for the new sound, and stayed small for the old one. After your child has said this, give the name: this is habituation, learning that a repeated sound is harmless. The full jump at the new sound shows the change belongs to the spoon only. If the volunteer also jumps a little more at the next spoon rings after the tin, that is called dishabituation. Real jumps are uneven, so a few ups and downs in the line are normal. If your results look different, say what you saw and why it may have happened. Nerves, a noisy room and a volunteer who tensed up can all change the scores.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Spoon Test. You draw the graph and say what you found.

experiments.title: Crammed or Spread Out: which way of learning lasts until tomorrow?
experiments.question: If you spend the same eight minutes learning a list of eight made-up words, do you remember more the next day if you learn it all at once, or in four short sittings spread through the day?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which list will you remember better tomorrow, the crammed list or the spread-out list? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both lists have eight pairs of words and are studied for the same eight minutes in total. Only the timing changes. One person crams list A and spreads list B. The second person crams list B and spreads list A, so that a harder list cannot fool us. Everyone is tested at the same time the next day.
results_table: Crammed list: words right out of 8
Spread list: words right out of 8
Which list was easier to learn?

materials.item: 16 small paper slips or cut-up card, with a made-up word on the front and its meaning on the back (the two lists are in the first step)
a clock or phone timer
two learners, for example your child and a parent
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.record: On day 2, write how many words each person got right from each list. Then write one sentence saying which way worked better for each person, and by how many words.
experiments.context: In this experiment two people learn two lists of made-up words in two different ways, and are tested the next day. You find out whether practice spread through a day lasts longer.

setup.art: Sixteen small paper slips laid out in two rows of eight. Each slip has a made-up word on the front, such as dabi, and a spoon drawn on the back.
setup.caption: 1. Make 16 slips: eight made-up words with meanings for list A, and eight for list B.

setup.art: A child and a parent sitting at a table with list A slips, looking at them for one minute, then saying the meanings aloud. A clock shows one minute.
setup.caption: 2. Crammed list: study it four times in a row, one minute looking and one minute saying.

setup.art: A day shown as four small pictures: morning sun, midday plate, afternoon tea, evening lamp, each with a slip pile being studied for two minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Spread list: study it four times, two minutes each, with at least an hour between sittings.

setup.art: The next morning, a child holding up the made-up word on a slip while a parent says the meaning, with a score table beside them.
setup.caption: 4. The next day, test both lists. Count the words right.

schedule.what: Make the slips. Cram one list in eight minutes. Study the other list in four short sittings through the day.
Test both lists and write the scores. Compare the two ways of learning.

flow.do: Make 16 slips, one for each made-up word and its meaning. List A has eight words. Dabi is a spoon. Nuko is a window. Fesa is a shoe. Ruma is a cloud. Tilo is a broom. Gavi is a lamp. Sepu is a coin. Hiku is a kite. List B has eight words. Mako is a pencil. Zeru is a bucket. Lopi is a tree. Wudi is a drum. Kete is a towel. Fuga is a key. Nafo is a moon. Rimo is a boat. Then write down each person's guess about which way of learning will work better.
flow.say: We will learn two lists of made-up words. One list we will learn all at once. One we will learn in short sittings through the day. Which will we remember better tomorrow, and why?
flow.kid: Make 16 slips from the two lists. Guess which way will work better. Why?

ask.q: Which way do you think will work better tomorrow, and why?
good: All at once, because you keep it fresh in your head.
Spread out, because your head gets time to rest between.
The same, because the time is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Each learner uses both lists, and the two learners test each other the next day. With 3 or 4 children, work in pairs. Person one crams list A and spreads list B. Person two crams list B and spreads list A.
flow.context: This is the first step of Crammed or Spread Out. You make the two lists and guess.

flow.do: Choose the list you will cram. Look at its slips for one minute. Then cover the meanings and say them aloud for one minute. Do this four times in a row, without a break.
flow.say: Look at all eight slips for one minute. Then cover the meanings and say them from memory for one minute. Do this four times in a row, with no break.
flow.kid: Look at the slips for one minute. Cover the meanings and say them. Do this four times.
flow.parent: Use a timer so that each learner studies for exactly eight minutes. Both learners cram at the same time, in different corners.

check.q: Why must the crammed list and the spread list each take exactly eight minutes?
options: So only the timing differs, not the amount of study
So the lists feel equally easy
check.why: If one list got more study time, it might be remembered better for that reason. With equal time, a difference comes from when the study happened.

flow.context: In this step you cram one list, with four rounds of study in a row.

flow.do: Study the other list in four sittings of two minutes each. Do the first sitting now. Do the next three later today. Leave at least an hour between sittings. Morning, lunch, afternoon and evening work well.
flow.say: This list gets four short sittings. Each time, look at the slips, cover the meanings, and say them. Remember to come back to it later today.
flow.kid: Study this list for two minutes. Come back three more times today. Wait an hour between sittings.
flow.parent: Put a note on the fridge to remind everyone about the sittings. If a sitting is missed, do it as soon as you remember and write the time. Do not study either list after bedtime, and do not look at the slips on day 2 before the test.
flow.context: In this step you study the second list in four short sittings through the day.

flow.do: The next day, test both lists. Show the made-up word on a slip, and ask for the meaning. Test the lists in a different order for each person. Score out of eight. Write each score in the table.
flow.say: Here is a made-up word. Tell me its meaning if you can. Do not worry if it has gone. We just want to see what stayed.
flow.kid: Show a made-up word. Ask for the meaning. Count how many are right.

ask.q: Which list stayed better, and does that match your guess?
good: The spread list stayed better.
The crammed list stayed better.
They were about the same.

flow.parent: Do not give hints. A difference of one word can happen by chance, because a list of eight is short. A difference of three or more across both learners is a clearer sign. If both lists score 7 or 8, the words were too easy to show a difference: test again three days later, without looking at the slips, and use those scores. If the lists came out equal, write that, and try again with a longer list on another day.
flow.context: In this step you test both lists the next day and count the words that stayed.

flow.do: Add up the scores for the crammed lists and for the spread lists. Draw two bars. Ask your child to say what they think the scores show, what they saw in the numbers, and why they think it came out this way.
flow.say: What do you think the scores show? What did you see in the numbers? Why do you think it came out this way?
flow.kid: Add up the scores for each way. Draw two bars. Say what you saw and why.
flow.think: If a sea slug can show the same pattern as you, what does that say about how learning works?
flow.parent: Many people remember more from the spread list, but not everyone does. After your child has given their reason, say that scientists have found the same in people, honeybees and sea slugs. Spaced practice usually lasts longer. One reason is that making a memory last takes the body time to build new parts, and a break gives that time.
flow.context: This is the last step of Crammed or Spread Out. You add up the scores and say what you found.

activities.title: What Have You Stopped Noticing?

materials.item: a quiet corner of the home
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess how many sounds there are, then count them in two rooms. List things touching your body, and find out what you had stopped noticing.

activities.record: The number of sounds you guessed and the number you counted in each room, a list of sounds you did not hear until you listened, and a list of five things touching your body that you had forgotten.
activities.context: In this short activity you find things around you that you had stopped noticing. It starts you thinking about how and why we stop noticing things.

setup.art: A child sitting very still with eyes closed on a sofa, with small pictures floating around: a ceiling fan, a fridge, a clock and a scooter outside.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still for 30 seconds with your eyes closed. Count every sound.

setup.art: A child looking at their own wrist, sleeve, collar, spectacles and the chair under them, each with a little arrow.
setup.caption: 2. List five things touching your body right now.

flow.do: First ask your child to guess how many different sounds they will hear in 30 seconds. Then they sit very still with their eyes closed for 30 seconds and count each different sound on their fingers. Write the guess and the count. Do the same in a second room. For example, use the kitchen and then a bedroom. Compare the two counts.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Count every sound you hear for 30 seconds. Count the quiet ones too.
flow.kid: Guess how many sounds. Sit very still, close your eyes and count for 30 seconds. Do it in two rooms.

ask.q: Which of those sounds were there ten minutes ago, but you did not hear them?
good: The fan.
The fridge.
The clock or the traffic.

flow.parent: Do not name any sounds. Just write down what your child says. Most homes have at least five sounds that nobody was hearing. With 2 to 4 children, each counts alone and writes their own list, then compare: did everyone hear the same sounds?
flow.context: In this step you guess, then listen for 30 seconds in two rooms and count the sounds in your home.

flow.do: Ask your child to name five things that are touching their body right now. Write the list. Examples are a collar, a watch strap, a waistband, spectacles and the seat.
flow.say: Now think about your body. What five things are touching you right now? A collar? A strap? The chair?
flow.kid: Name five things touching your body now. Write them down.

ask.q: Which of these did you notice before I asked?
good: None of them.
Only the chair.
Only one or two.

flow.parent: A few children will feel each of these things as soon as they think of them. That is the point: the feeling was there all along.
flow.context: In this step you list things touching your body that you had stopped feeling.

flow.do: Ask your child where the fan sound went when they were not hearing it. Let them answer in their own words. Then ask the question in the check.
flow.say: When you were not hearing the fan, where was the sound? Was it gone? Did your ears stop working? What do you think?
flow.kid: Where was the fan sound when you did not hear it? What do you think?

check.q: You did not hear the fridge until you listened. What is the best explanation?
options: The sound was there, but your mind had stopped reacting to it
The sound switched off until you listened
check.why: The sound reached your ears all the time. Your mind had learned that the sound does not matter, and stopped reacting. Listening on purpose brought it back. 'Your ears turned off' is a common idea, but ears do not switch off.

flow.think: Is getting used to something a kind of learning?
flow.parent: This is the question for the whole unit. Do not answer it. The Spoon Test will let your child find out.
flow.context: In this step you ask where a sound goes when you stop hearing it.

activities.title: The Meerkat Lesson: how much does teaching cost?

materials.item: 8 sheets of A4 paper or newspaper pages cut to a rectangle
a clock or phone timer
a parent or friend who does not yet know the fold you will teach

schedule.what: Time yourself making a paper boat alone. Teach a parent in three steps, from easy to hard. Compare the times.

activities.record: The time you took alone, the time you took teaching, and how many tries your learner needed.
activities.context: In this activity you teach someone a paper fold, the way meerkat helpers teach their pups. You find out whether teaching costs the teacher something.

setup.art: A child folding a paper boat quickly alone at a table while a timer shows the seconds.
setup.caption: 1. Time yourself folding a paper boat alone.

setup.art: A child handing a parent a paper boat folded all but the last two folds, with a plain sheet and a half-folded boat beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Teach in three steps. First hand over a nearly finished boat, then a half-folded one, then a plain sheet.

setup.art: A child and a parent looking at two numbers on paper: the seconds taken alone and the seconds taken to teach.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the time you took alone with the time you took to teach.

flow.do: Pick a fold your child can make but a parent does not know. Most adults know the plain paper boat. If the parent knows it, use a jumping frog or a tulip instead, and read 'boat' in these steps as that fold. Time your child making it alone. Write the seconds.
flow.say: Make the paper boat as fast as you neatly can, all alone. I will time you.
flow.kid: Make a paper boat all alone. Ask a grown-up to time you.
flow.parent: If your child does not know a fold yet, spend five minutes learning one from a video first. Choose a fold that takes about a minute.
flow.context: In this step you time yourself making a paper boat alone.

flow.do: Teach a parent in three levels. For level one, give them a boat with all but the last two folds done. For level two, give them a half-folded boat. For level three, give them a plain sheet. Help only when they are stuck. Time all three levels.
flow.say: Here is a nearly finished boat. Finish it. Now a half-finished one. Now a plain sheet. I will help only when you are stuck.
flow.kid: Hand over a nearly done boat first. Then a half-done one. Then a plain sheet.

ask.q: What did you do to help your learner, that you do not do when you fold alone?
good: I slowed down.
I waited when they were stuck.
I made it easier first.

flow.parent: Meerkat helpers do the same. They first give young pups dead scorpions, then crippled ones, then live ones. Do not tell your child this yet. Let them notice what they did as the teacher. Time each level and add them up. With 2 to 4 children, one teaches, one or two learn, and one times. For a fair comparison with two learners, teach one in the three levels, and let the other only watch the fold once at full speed. Then both learners try a plain sheet. Who finishes faster?
flow.context: In this step you teach a parent a fold in three levels, from easy to hard.

flow.do: Compare the time your child took alone with the total time they took teaching. If you had two learners, compare how fast the taught learner and the watch-once learner folded a plain sheet. Ask what teaching cost the teacher, and what it gave the learner.
flow.say: How long did it take you alone? How long did it take to teach me? What did teaching cost you?
flow.kid: Compare the two times. What did teaching cost you?

check.q: A teacher spends extra time and effort so that a learner learns faster. Who pays the cost?
options: The teacher, who gives up time and effort
The learner, who has to wait
check.why: Teaching costs the teacher. A meerkat helper gives up a scorpion meal, and an ant leader walks slowly. That cost is one reason scientists say teaching is rare.

flow.parent: Teaching took longer than doing, and that is the point. In animals, scientists look for three things: the teacher changes what she does only when a learner is there, it costs her something, and the learner learns faster.
flow.context: In this step you compare the time alone with the time spent teaching.

activities.title: One Time Is Enough: a family survey

materials.item: paper and a pencil
five people to ask, in person or by phone

schedule.what: Make a table. Ask five people two questions. Look for a pattern in the number of tries.

activities.record: A table with five rows. Each row has a name, a food or smell they avoid after one bad time, and how many tries it took to learn a skill like riding a cycle.
activities.context: In this activity you ask five people how many bad times it took before they started avoiding a food, and how many tries it took them to learn a skill. You look for which kind of learning is faster.

setup.art: A child with a notebook asking a grandmother two questions while she holds a cup of tea.
setup.caption: 1. Ask five people the two questions.

setup.art: A table in a notebook with columns: name, food avoided, tries to learn the food, tries to learn a skill.
setup.caption: 2. Write each answer in your table.

flow.do: Draw a table with five rows and four columns. The columns are name, food or smell avoided, how many bad times it took to start avoiding it, and how many tries it took to learn a skill. Write the two questions at the top. Before asking, guess which kind of learning took fewer tries.
flow.say: Question one: Is there a food or smell you avoid because it once made you feel unwell? Question two: How many tries did it take you to learn a skill like riding a cycle?
flow.kid: Draw the table. Write two questions at the top.
flow.parent: Tell your child to ask only people who are happy to answer, and not to ask for details of any illness. A food that once upset a stomach is enough.
flow.context: In this step you set up the table for the family survey.

flow.do: Your child asks five people the two questions and writes the answers. For the food, ask how many times it made them unwell before they started avoiding it. For the skill, ask roughly how many tries it took.
flow.say: Ask each person the two questions. For the food, ask how many times it made them unwell before they started avoiding it. For the skill, ask roughly how many tries it took.
flow.kid: Ask five people. Write how many times it took for each.

ask.q: What do you notice about how many times each kind of learning took?
good: The food took once.
The skill took many tries.
The food was learned much faster.

flow.parent: Many people will say the food took one time, and the skill took many tries. Some people do not recall. Write 'not sure' and move on. If five people are not at home, phone relatives, or let brothers and sisters pool their answers: each child asks two or three people, and you combine the tables.
flow.context: In this step you ask five people and write down their answers.

flow.do: Count how many people learned the food in one go. Count how many skills took more than ten tries. Ask your child what they notice.
flow.say: Look at your table. How many people learned the food in one go? How many needed many tries for the skill? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Count the one-go foods. Count the many-tries skills. What do you notice?
flow.think: Why might a body be ready to learn some links in just one go?
flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain that scientists call this taste aversion. A body is ready to link a taste with feeling ill, even a long time later, because that link can save a life. John Garcia and Robert Koelling showed in 1966 that animals link taste with illness easily, but not a flash of light with illness.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Time Is Enough. You look for a pattern in the answers.

projects.title: The Appointment: do the visitors learn the time?

materials.item: a small dish of broken rice and a bowl of clean water, to put on the same ledge or balcony every day
a notebook and a pencil
a clock or phone that shows the time

projects.safety: Put out only plain broken rice or grain and clean water, with no salty, oily or sweet food. Wash the dish and bowl each day. Do not touch the visitors, and wash your hands afterwards. If the ledge is high or has no railing, a grown-up puts the dish out. Your child must never lean over or climb on a ledge. Keep the dish where you can see it. If monkeys, stray dogs or snakes come near, stop feeding, move away and tell a grown-up. Empty and refill the water every day so that mosquitoes cannot breed in it, and check that your building allows feeding birds.

schedule.what: Choose a ledge and a time. For 20 minutes before that time, write down who visits with no food out. Then put out the dish and water, and write the time any visitor first arrives.
Put out the dish at the same time. Sit near the window from 10 minutes before until 20 minutes after, and write the time the first visitor arrives.
Same time, same ledge. Sit near the window from 10 minutes before until 20 minutes after, and write when the first visitor arrives.
Same time, same ledge. Sit near the window from 10 minutes before until 20 minutes after, and write when the first visitor arrives.
Same time, same ledge. Sit near the window from 10 minutes before until 20 minutes after, and write when the first visitor arrives.
Put out nothing. Watch the ledge for 30 minutes around the usual time. Write who comes, and when.
Draw a graph of the arrival times and say what you found.

projects.record: A table with seven rows: day, time food was put out, time the first visitor arrived, and who came. Then a line graph of the arrival times.
projects.context: In this project you feed the same visitors at the same time for five days, then put out nothing on day six. You find out whether they come at the time anyway. It is for families with a balcony, ledge or garden where birds or squirrels visit.

setup.art: A small steel dish of broken rice and a bowl of water on a balcony ledge, with a wall clock showing seven thirty in the background.
setup.caption: 1. Put the dish and water on the same ledge at the same time each day.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook and a pencil, watching a crow on the ledge.
setup.caption: 2. Watch from a distance. Write the time the first visitor arrives.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of seven rows and a small line graph of arrival times beside it.
setup.caption: 3. On day seven, draw a graph of the arrival times.

flow.do: Choose a ledge, balcony or garden spot that birds or squirrels already visit. Choose a time, such as 7:30 in the morning. For 20 minutes before that time, with no food out, write down who visits. Then put out the dish and water at that time. Write when the first visitor arrives.
flow.say: We will feed whoever visits, at exactly the same time every day. Then we will see if they learn the time. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Pick a ledge and a time. Put out rice and water. Write when anyone arrives.

ask.q: Will the visitors start to come at the same time each day? Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because they learn when the food comes.
No, because they do not know what a clock is.
They will come earlier each day.

flow.parent: If nobody visits in three days, move the dish to a more open ledge, or watch a neighbour's regular visitor, a street dog at a gate, or a family pet instead. Do not change the time once you choose it.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Appointment. You choose the time and put out the first dish.

flow.do: On days two to five, put out the dish and water at the same time. Sit near the window from 10 minutes before until 20 minutes after, doing something quiet. Write the time the first visitor arrives, and who it is.
flow.say: Put out the dish at the same time again. Watch from a distance. Write when the first visitor comes.
flow.kid: Put the dish out at the same time. Write when the first visitor comes.
flow.parent: Visitors may start to arrive earlier and then settle closer to the feeding time. Five days is short, so there may be no clear change; if so, say that, or carry on for ten days. With 2 to 4 children, one puts out the dish, one watches the clock, one writes. For a group, each can watch a different ledge or a different kind of visitor. Some days nobody comes, and that is a result too. Write it as it is.
flow.context: In this step you repeat the feeding and the watching on days two to five.

flow.do: On day six, put out nothing. Watch the ledge from 15 minutes before the usual time until 15 minutes after. Write who comes, and when.
flow.say: Today we put out nothing. We just watch. Will anybody come at the usual time?
flow.kid: Put out nothing today. Watch the ledge for 30 minutes. Write who comes.
flow.think: If a visitor comes at the usual time with no food, what had they learned?
flow.parent: Some visitors will come, look and leave. Others will not come. Both are fine. Put the food back on day seven so that nobody goes hungry.
flow.context: In this step you put out nothing and see whether the visitors come at the usual time.

flow.do: Draw a line graph with the day along the bottom and the arrival time up the side. Mark day six. Ask your child to say what they think happened, what the arrival times show, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What do the arrival times show? Why do you think the visitors came, or did not come, on day six?
flow.kid: Draw a graph of the arrival times. Say what you saw and why.
flow.parent: Scientists have shown that honeybees learn the time of day for a feeder. Ingeborg Beling did this in 1929. Birds and mammals do it too. Your result may be messier than hers, and that is fine. Say what you saw.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Appointment. You draw the graph and say what you found.

challenges.title: A Signal Nobody Ignores
challenges.problem: A farmer's bird scarer makes the same sound every ten minutes, and the birds have stopped caring. Design a pattern of sounds that people still notice after 20 sounds, and test it against a steady sound.
constraints: Use only things from home, such as a steel plate and spoon, a rice tin, a cycle bell and a clap.
The gap between sounds must be 15 seconds every time, so only the pattern changes.
Test your pattern on one volunteer and the steady spoon on another volunteer, using the scoring card from the Spoon Test.
Make 20 sounds for your pattern and 20 for the steady spoon, and write down every score.
materials: a steel plate and spoon, a tin of rice, and a cycle bell or another sound maker
the scoring card from the Spoon Test
general: Change the loudness of the ring: soft, medium and loud in a fixed order.
Use two sounds, and swap between them in a regular pattern.
Make the sound louder as time passes, so that each one is a little new.
creative: Roll a die before each sound to choose which of four sounds to make, so that nobody can predict the next one.
Add a rare sound that only comes once in a long while, to bring the attention back.
Change the place you stand, as well as the sound, because the place can be new too.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your pattern and test it on one volunteer, with the steady spoon on another. Compare the scores after 20 sounds. Which scores stayed higher for longer? Change one thing and test again.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about getting used to sounds. You use what you learned in the Spoon Test to build a signal that people keep noticing.

setup.art: A child sketching four sound ideas on paper, with small drawings of a plate, a bell, a tin and a clap, and a die beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch your sound pattern. Choose four sounds.

setup.art: A child rolling a die and ringing one of four sounds behind a volunteer who is doing a puzzle.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die to choose each sound. Ring it behind the volunteer.

setup.art: Two line graphs side by side on paper, one for the steady spoon that drops low and one for the dice pattern that stays higher.
setup.caption: 3. Draw both scores on graphs. Compare them.

flow.do: Read the problem. Ask your child to choose four sounds from home and sketch a pattern for 20 sounds. They could use a die to choose each sound.
flow.say: A farmer's bird scarer made the same sound every ten minutes, and the birds stopped caring. How could you make a sound pattern that people keep noticing? Sketch some ideas first.
flow.kid: Choose four sounds from home. Sketch a pattern for 20 sounds.

ask.q: Why did the birds stop caring about the scarer?
good: It was always the same.
It never hurt them.
They learned it was harmless.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Signal challenge. You plan your pattern.

flow.do: Test your pattern on one volunteer: 20 sounds, 15 seconds apart. Then test the steady spoon on another volunteer in the same way. Score every sound with the Spoon Test card.
flow.say: Please do your puzzle. Sounds will come from behind you. (Say this to the first volunteer before your pattern, and to the second volunteer before the steady spoon.)
flow.kid: Ring your pattern 20 times behind one volunteer. Ring the steady spoon behind another. Score each.
flow.parent: Pick volunteers who agree and who are not startled by sudden sounds. Follow the Spoon Test safety rules: nothing close to an ear, and no babies or anyone with a heart problem. Choose gentle volume for every sound. It is a fair test only if both volunteers sit the same way and do the same kind of puzzle. Even then, the two volunteers are different people. Write that down, and say why it matters.
flow.context: In this step you test your pattern and the steady spoon on two volunteers.

flow.do: Draw a line graph of the scores for each volunteer. Compare the scores for sounds 10 to 20. Ask your child which pattern was ignored sooner, and why.
flow.say: Look at the two graphs. Which volunteer started ignoring the sounds first? Why do you think so? What would you change?
flow.kid: Draw both graphs. Which pattern was ignored sooner? Why?
flow.think: Could a pattern ever be so unpredictable that nobody gets used to it?
flow.parent: The pattern often keeps scores higher for longer, but it can also be ignored once all four sounds have been heard many times. The two volunteers are also different people, and that can change the scores. Say what you saw.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Signal challenge. You compare the two graphs.
