quiz.p: What does learning mean for a living being?
opts: A lasting change in what she does, caused by experience
Any movement at all
Something that only happens at school
quiz.why: Learning is a change caused by experience that lasts. A reflex is not learning, and neither is growing.

quiz.p: You stop hearing a fan after a while. What is happening?
opts: Your mind has learned the sound does not matter
Your ears have stopped working
The fan has become quieter
quiz.why: The sound still reaches your ears. Your mind has learned to leave it out, which is habituation.

quiz.p: A new sound can bring back a reaction that had grown weak.
quiz.why: True. This is dishabituation. It shows that only the old sound had been learned as harmless.

quiz.p: Which result shows that a drop in response is habituation and not tiredness?
opts: A new stimulus brings the response back at full strength
The response is weakest at the end
The being lies still
quiz.why: A tired being reacts less to everything. A strong reaction to something new shows the drop belongs to the old stimulus.

quiz.p: Why can a person avoid a food for years after one bad meal?
opts: Bodies are ready to link a taste with feeling ill, even in one go
The food changes after one meal
Taste is never learned
quiz.why: A link between a taste and feeling ill can save a life, so bodies form it fast and keep it.

quiz.p: Honeybees can learn flower colours, smells and the ____ of day when food appears.
a: time
quiz.why: Honeybees fed at the same time each day come at that time on later days, even with no food.

quiz.p: Which living thing has been shown to get used to a harmless bitter bridge?
opts: A slime mould, which has no nerve cells
A stone
A dead leaf
quiz.why: Slime moulds are single giant cells, and they can stop avoiding a harmless bitter bridge. Only living things can do this.

quiz.p: Which way of learning a list of words usually lasts longer?
opts: Short sittings spread over a day or more
One long sitting
A sitting just before the test
quiz.why: Spaced practice gives the body time to build a lasting change. Sea slugs, bees and people all show this.

quiz.p: In animal teaching, the teacher pays a cost, such as time.
quiz.why: True. A leader ant slows down and waits, and a meerkat helper gives up a meal. The cost is one of the three signs of teaching.

quiz.p: What do meerkat helpers do as the pups grow older?
opts: Give them scorpions that are more alive and harder to handle
Stop feeding them
Give them the same dead scorpions
quiz.why: Helpers give young pups dead scorpions, then scorpions that are crippled, and live ones as the pups get older. The lessons get harder as the pups get better.

quiz.p: In a sea slug, what happens at the synapse when a gentle touch is repeated many times?
opts: The touch-sensing cell releases less chemical
The cell grows a new arm
Nothing changes
quiz.why: Less chemical crosses the gap, so the gill pulls in less. This is how Kandel's team traced a simple learned change to one connection.

quiz.p: Learning can change the physical connections between nerve cells.
quiz.why: True. In sea slugs, and in people such as taxi drivers learning streets, learning leaves a physical mark.

worksheets.title: Getting Used To It, Linking and Teaching (core)

items.p: Which of these is learning?
opts: A sparrow stops fleeing from a scarecrow that never moves
A baby bird opens her beak when a parent lands on the nest
A chick's legs getting stronger as she grows
items.why: Learning is a change caused by experience that lasts. The sparrow changed because of what she saw each day. The beak opening is ready at hatching, and stronger legs come from growing, not from experience.

items.p: When you stop hearing the fridge, your ears have stopped working.
items.why: False. The sound still reaches your ears. Your mind has learned that the sound does not matter, and stopped reacting to it. If you listen on purpose, you hear it again.

items.p: The simplest kind of learning, where the response to a repeated harmless sound gets weaker, is called ____.
a: habituation
getting used to it
items.why: Habituation is a lasting drop in how strongly a being reacts to something that keeps happening and does no harm.

items.p: In the Spoon Test, a volunteer who had stopped jumping at the spoon still jumped at the rice tin. What does this show?
opts: Only the spoon sound had been learned as harmless, so the volunteer was not just tired
The rice tin is always louder than a spoon
The volunteer was trying to be funny
items.why: A tired person would react less to every sound. The jump at a new sound shows that only the old sound had been learned as harmless.

items.p: Put these in order to show what happens with a scarecrow over a week.
a: Birds meet a new scarecrow and keep far away
Every day the scarecrow stands still and nothing happens
Birds come a little closer each day
A sparrow sits on the scarecrow's head
The farmer moves the scarecrow and changes the signals
items.why: Birds first fear what is new. Each harmless day teaches them it does not matter, so they come closer. A farmer who changes things makes the scarecrow new again.

items.p: Sort each situation by the kind of learning.
items: You stop hearing a clock that ticks all day
Bees return to blue flowers that gave nectar
A dog stops barking at the hum of a fridge
A cat runs at the sound of a tin being opened
A sparrow sits on a scarecrow that never moves
A child avoids a food that once made her ill
items.a: as given
items.why: In getting used to it, a being learns that something repeated is harmless. In linking, a being learns that two things go together, such as a flower colour and nectar.

items.p: Match each living thing to something they can learn.
pairs: Sea slug
To ignore a gentle touch that never hurts
Honeybee
The time of day when food appears
Meerkat pup
To handle a scorpion, with help from adults
Young songbird
A song, by hearing adults
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Animals learn many different things. Even a sea slug with 20,000 nerve cells learns, and so does a bee with about a million.

items.p: In two sentences, say why a farmer who wants to scare birds should keep changing the scarecrow.
items.a: Birds get used to a scarecrow that never changes and never hurts them. A changed scarecrow is new again, so the birds react to it again.
items.why: A strong answer says that birds learn a repeated harmless thing does not matter, and that a new thing brings the reaction back.

items.p: Here is a drawing of the Spoon Test. Label the three parts: the volunteer, the plate and spoon, and the scoring card.
labels: Sits facing away, doing a puzzle
items.art: A volunteer sitting at a table doing a puzzle, facing away. A child stands behind with a plate and spoon, and a scoring card lies on a table.
a: Sits facing away, doing a puzzle: the volunteer
Rings once every 15 seconds: the plate and spoon
Has 0, 1 and 2 on it: the scoring card
items.why: The volunteer does a puzzle and faces away, so each sound is a surprise. The tester rings the plate and spoon at equal gaps, and scores each jump with the same card.

items.p: Only animals with a big brain can learn.
items.why: False. A sea slug has about 20,000 nerve cells, and a honeybee about a million. Both learn. A human brain has about 86 billion.

items.p: A child is ill an hour after eating brinjal curry and refuses brinjal for years. What kind of learning is this?
opts: Linking a taste with feeling ill, in one go
Getting used to the taste of brinjal
Copying a sister who also refuses it
items.why: Bodies are ready to link a taste with feeling ill, even when the illness comes a long time later, and even after just one time. This protects against food that may harm.

items.p: A sea slug pulls in the gill when touched. After many gentle touches, the pull gets ____.
a: weaker
smaller
items.why: The slug has learned that the gentle touch is harmless, so the pull gets weaker.

items.p: Draw a line graph of a volunteer's jumps for 12 spoon rings, then one rice-tin shake, then one more spoon ring.
items.a: A line that starts high, around 2, falls to near 0 by ring 8 to 12, jumps up at the rice tin, and then falls to 0 at the last spoon ring.
items.why: The fall shows getting used to the spoon. The jump at the tin shows the person is not just tired. The low last point shows the spoon is still ignored.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why: a spider spinning her first web, a baby sucking milk, a crow in Japan dropping nuts on a road for cars to crack, a newborn blinking at bright light?
items.a: The crow. The other three are ready at birth. The crow's trick was learned from experience.
items.why: A spider's first web, a baby's sucking and a blink are built in. Dropping nuts on a road for cars is learned from experience, and other crows seem to pick it up by watching.

items.p: A sparrow sits on the clay-pot head of a scarecrow.

views.says: The sparrow is foolish. She should still be afraid.
The sparrow has learned that the scarecrow never hurts her. That is learning.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What would you check?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. It may suggest checking whether the sparrow still flees a hawk or a new object.
items.why: Both views try to explain the same fact. A way to check them is to see whether the sparrow reacts to something new. If she does, she has learned about this scarecrow only.

items.p: Honeybees fed at a window at four o'clock for five days come at four o'clock on day six, when there is no food. What does this show?
opts: Bees can learn the time of day when food appears
Bees can read a clock
Bees only come when they smell food
items.why: The bees came at four o'clock, with no food or smell to bring them. So they had learned the time of day. Ingeborg Beling found this in 1929.

items.p: Which result would show that a drop in jumping is tiredness and not habituation?
opts: The person also stops jumping at a brand new sound
The person jumps again at a new sound
The jumps are smallest at the end
items.why: A tired person would react less to every sound. If a new sound brings the jump back, the person is not just tired.

items.p: After a loud thunderclap, a dog who now jumps at small sounds is showing sensitisation.
items.why: True. Sensitisation is a rise in how strongly a being reacts, after a strong or scary event.

items.p: What is dishabituation?
opts: A new stimulus bringing back a response that had grown weak
Forgetting what you learned
Getting used to two sounds at once
items.why: Dishabituation is the return of a response when something new happens. It is one sign that the earlier drop was learned.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Habituation
Reacting less to a repeated harmless sound
Dishabituation
A new sound bringing the reaction back
Sensitisation
Reacting more strongly after a scary event
Association
Learning that two things go together
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words describe different ways that experience changes how strongly a being reacts or what she expects.

items.p: Put these in order, for a sea slug getting used to a gentle touch.
a: The siphon (a small spout on the slug's body) is touched gently
The touch-sensing cell sends a message across a synapse
The message makes the muscle pull in the gill
The touch is repeated many times
The touch-sensing cell releases less chemical, so the pull is weaker
items.why: A touch starts a message that crosses a synapse to a muscle cell. After many harmless touches, less chemical crosses the gap, and the pull gets weaker.

items.p: The tiny gap where one nerve cell passes a chemical message to the next is called a ____.
a: synapse
items.why: A synapse is the gap between two nerve cells. Learning changes how strongly it passes the message.

items.p: A friend says that a person who stops jumping at a spoon must simply be tired. In two sentences, explain how a rice tin could show this is wrong.
items.a: A tired person would not jump at a new sound either. If the person jumps at the rice tin, the old spoon sound alone was learned as harmless.
items.why: A strong answer says tiredness would lower every response, and that a strong response to something new shows the person is still alert.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why: a meerkat helper giving a pup a crippled scorpion, a leader ant waiting for a follower, a crow watching another crow open a nut?
items.a: The crow watching. In the other two, the animal changes what she does for the learner, at a cost to herself.
items.why: Teaching needs the teacher to change her behaviour for a learner. The crow who watches is learning, but the crow who is watched is not teaching.

items.p: Sort each by whether the skill is built in from birth or learned.
items: A spider spinning her first web
A newborn blinking at bright light
A bee finding nectar at four o'clock
A young finch singing his father's song
items.a: as given
items.why: Reflexes and first webs are ready at birth. Skills that depend on experience, such as a time of day or a song, are learned.

items.p: A bee gets nectar from 6 of the first 8 flowers. The paying colour then changes, and she gets nectar from 2 of the next 8. She then gets nectar from 6 of the last 8. Draw a line graph with three points.
items.a: A line that starts at 6, dips to 2, and rises back to 6.
items.why: The dip shows the bee still picking the old colour just after the change. The rise shows she learned the new colour.

items.p: Why is it interesting that slime moulds get used to a harmless bitter bridge?
opts: They have no nerve cells, so a learning-like change can happen without them
They are the biggest animals alive
They move faster than any other living thing
items.why: Slime moulds are single giant cells with no nerve cells. A change that is kept and belongs to one substance happens in them too. Scientists argue about whether to call it learning.

items.p: A person gets 3 of 8 words right from a crammed list and 6 of 8 from a list learned in spaced sittings. How many more words did the spaced list give?
items.why: 6 minus 3 is 3. The spaced list gave 3 more words, which is twice as many.

items.p: Slime moulds get used to a harmless bitter bridge after some days, and no nerve cells are involved.

views.says: This is learning. The change is kept and belongs to one substance, just as in a sea slug.
This is a simple chemical change in the cell. The word learning is best kept for animals with nerve cells.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What would you test to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side or a middle path and gives a reason. It may suggest testing whether the change is kept for days and belongs to one substance.
items.why: Both views agree on what the slime mould does. They differ on the word learning. If the slime mould passes the same tests as a sea slug, the first view gets stronger.

items.p: A farm uses a bird scarer that booms exactly every ten minutes. Say what will happen after a week, and why.
items.a: The birds will get used to it and come back to the field. The boom is always the same and never hurts them, so they learn it does not matter.
items.why: A strong answer says the sound is repeated and harmless, so birds get used to it. It may suggest that a random or changing sound would last longer.

items.p: Only animals with a brain have ever been shown to get used to a repeated harmless touch.
items.why: False. Stentor, a one-celled animal, and slime moulds, which are single giant cells, have been shown to stop reacting to repeated harmless things. Scientists argue about what to call this.

items.p: Here is a drawing of two nerve cells. Label the touch-sensing cell, the gap between the cells, and the cell that makes the muscle move.
labels: Receives the message from the skin
Sends the message to the gill muscle
items.art: Two nerve cells joined by a small gap, with chemical dots crossing it. One cell is attached to a patch of skin and the other to a muscle.
a: Receives the message from the skin: the touch-sensing cell
Where the chemical crosses: the synapse
Sends the message to the gill muscle: the motor cell
items.why: A touch is sensed by one cell, which sends a chemical across the synapse to the motor cell, which makes the muscle move. Learning changes how much chemical crosses.

items.p: Design a doorbell for a hospital ward that nurses will keep noticing for a whole year. Say what rule it follows, and why.
items.a: The bell changes its sound in an unpredictable way, such as choosing from four sounds at random. People get used to a sound that stays the same, so a changing sound keeps being new.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that a repeated, harmless stimulus is ignored, and that change or surprise brings attention back. It may also add that a rare, important sound can stay the same.

items.p: Why did scientists who wanted to trace a simple learned change to single cells choose a sea slug?
opts: The slug has few nerve cells and they are large, so one pathway can be followed
Sea slugs are the cleverest animals
Mammals cannot be touched
items.why: A sea slug has about 20,000 nerve cells, and some are large enough to see. A human brain has about 86 billion. A small, clear pathway made the change easy to follow.

items.p: In a famous test, thirsty rats drank sweet water, and a light flashed and a click sounded as they drank. Some rats were later made unwell. The unwell rats avoided the sweet water afterwards, but not the flash and click. What does this show?
opts: Animals are ready to link some things more easily than others
Rats cannot learn
Flashes are always scarier than tastes
items.why: A taste is a likely cause of feeling ill, but a flash is not. Bodies are ready for the likely links, which can keep them alive.

items.p: A meerkat helper gives a pup a scorpion with the stinger removed.

views.says: This is teaching. The helper changes what she gives, it costs her a meal, and the pup learns faster.
We cannot be sure this is teaching. We do not know that the helper understands what the pup does not know.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What evidence would settle it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. It may say that the three tests are met but that we cannot see what the helper knows.
items.why: Both views agree on what the helper does. They differ on what teaching needs. Scientists still argue about this.

items.p: If a memory is held in the connections between cells, then it must sit in exactly one nerve cell.
items.why: False. A connection is between two cells, and a memory probably involves many connections. Scientists still argue about how a memory is spread.

items.p: Put these steps in order, for the test that tells habituation apart from tiredness.
a: Ring the spoon until the jumps get small
Make a new sound
Score the jump at the new sound
Ring the spoon again and score it
Compare the scores for the two sounds
items.why: First the response is lowered by repeats. Then a new stimulus is tried, and the old one is tried again. A big response to the new one and a small response to the old one shows the change belongs to the old sound.

items.p: If a being ignores one sound but reacts to a new one, the change belongs to that one sound only. We say the change is ____ to the sound.
a: specific
items.why: The change belongs to one stimulus only. This is one of the signs that separate learning from tiredness.

items.p: The chart shows made-up scores for a volunteer. Explain in three sentences what the first 12 bars show and what the 13th bar shows.

chart.title: Made-up scores for one volunteer: 12 spoon rings, a rice tin, and the spoon again

items.context: In the Spoon Test, you scored each jump of a volunteer. These are made-up scores in the same test.
items.a: The first 12 bars fall from 2 to 0, so the person got used to the spoon. The 13th bar is 2, so a new sound brought the jump back. The 14th bar is 0, so the spoon was still ignored.
items.why: A strong answer reads the fall as habituation, the 13th bar as dishabituation, and the low last bar as specific to the spoon.

items.p: Draw a model of two nerve cells before and after many gentle touches. Show what changes at the gap.
items.a: Two cells with a gap. Before: many chemical dots cross the gap. After: fewer dots cross the gap.
items.why: The change that Kandel's team found was less chemical crossing the synapse. Models are drawings that explain, so any clear picture of fewer dots crossing is a good answer.

items.p: Many of the molecules at a synapse are replaced within days or weeks, yet some memories last for decades. What does this suggest?
opts: The memory may be a pattern that continues while the parts are replaced
The memory must be held in the molecules that never change
Memories do not really last for decades
items.why: Scientists have long wondered about this puzzle. One idea is that a memory is a pattern or process, and not a thing, so it can continue as the parts change. It is still debated.

items.p: Sort each claim by how sure scientists are.
items: Learning changes the connections between nerve cells
Plants such as the touch-me-not learn
A sea slug can get used to a gentle touch

items.p: A bee gets nectar from 6 of 8 flowers in block 1, 2 of 8 in block 2, and 7 of 8 in block 3. What fraction of all 24 flowers gave her nectar? Write it in its simplest form.
items.why: 6 plus 2 plus 7 is 15. So 15 of 24 flowers gave nectar. Dividing both numbers by 3 gives 5 out of 8.

items.p: Give two reasons why it helps an animal to get used to harmless sounds.

items.p: A touch-me-not plant stops folding the leaves when dropped again and again. Which later result would help show that the plant had learned, and was not just tired?

The plant folds the leaves even more at the drop after a rest
The plant stops moving altogether
items.why: Learning is kept after a rest and belongs to one stimulus. Tiredness would pass with rest and would affect every touch.

open_questions.q: Where exactly is a memory kept?
open_questions.why_open: In mice, switching on cells that were active during an event can bring a memory back. Other results suggest that a memory is spread across many cells, and can shift over time.

open_questions.q: How can a memory last for decades when the molecules at a synapse are replaced within days or weeks?
open_questions.why_open: Francis Crick pointed out this puzzle in 1984. One idea is that a memory is a pattern that continues while its parts are replaced. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Do slime moulds, one-celled swimmers and plants learn in the same sense as animals with nerve cells?
open_questions.why_open: The changes they show pass the same tests as getting used to a touch in a sea slug. Scientists argue about whether to call these changes learning.

open_questions.q: Do any animals teach while knowing what the learner does not know?
open_questions.why_open: Meerkat helpers and ants pass the three tests of teaching. We cannot ask them what they understand.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a sea slug to get used to a touch?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can ask a sea slug, and we have no test for what it is like inside. Whether there is any feeling at all is an open question.

maths.problem: The bar chart shows made-up scores for twelve spoon rings: 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0. Add the first six scores, and then the last six. By how many points did the total fall?
maths.answer: The total fell by 8 points, from 10 to 2.
maths.explain: The first six scores are 2, 2, 2, 1, 2 and 1, which add to 10. The last six are 1, 0, 1, 0, 0 and 0, which add to 2. 10 take away 2 is 8. The jumps got much smaller.

chart.title: Made-up scores for twelve spoon rings

maths.context: In the Spoon Test, you scored each jump of a volunteer. These are made-up scores for twelve rings.
maths.why_maths: Adding the scores in two halves is a quick way to see whether the jumps got smaller.

maths.problem: In made-up Spoon Test scores, the first six rings add to 10 points and the last six add to 2 points. What fraction of the first total is left? Write it in its simplest form.
maths.explain: 2 out of 10 is 2 tenths. Dividing the top and bottom by 2 gives 1 out of 5. So only one fifth of the jumping is left.
maths.context: In the Spoon Test, a volunteer's jump scores fall as the spoon is rung again and again. These are made-up totals.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of the reaction is left, and it is easier to compare between volunteers than two raw totals.

maths.problem: One person got 3 words right from the crammed list and 6 from the spread-out list, out of 8 each. How many times as many words did the spread-out list give? What does this suggest?
maths.answer: Twice as many. The spread-out list gave 6 words and the crammed list gave 3.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 3 is 2. The spread-out list gave twice as many words. With only eight words, one person's result could be luck, so more learners would make the answer stronger.
maths.context: In Crammed or Spread Out, two people learn two lists of words in two different ways, and are tested the next day.
maths.why_maths: A ratio compares two results with one number, and shows how large the difference is.

maths.problem: In The Appointment, a crow was fed at 7:30 am each day. On day six no food was put out. The crow came at 7:20 am and left at 7:55 am. How many minutes was the crow there before 7:30, and how many after 7:30? How long was the crow there in all?
maths.answer: 10 minutes before 7:30, 25 minutes after, and 35 minutes in all.
maths.explain: From 7:20 to 7:30 is 10 minutes. From 7:30 to 7:55 is 25 minutes. 10 plus 25 is 35 minutes. The crow was waiting around the learned feeding time.
maths.context: In The Appointment, visitors are fed at the same time every day and you see whether they come at that time with no food.
maths.why_maths: Working out how long a visitor stays around the usual time shows how exactly an animal has learned the time.

maths.problem: A die has six faces. You pick sound 1, 2, 3 or 4 when the die shows that number, and roll again on a 5 or a 6. What is the chance that the next sound is the same as the last one?
maths.explain: Each roll that counts gives one of four sounds, and each is equally likely. The chance of the same sound again is 1 out of 4. A pattern like this is hard for the birds to predict.
maths.context: In the Signal challenge, you pick which sound to ring by rolling a die, so that nobody can guess the next one.
maths.why_maths: A chance shows how unpredictable a signal is, and a signal that is hard to predict is harder to get used to.

maths.problem: Look at your own Spoon Test scores. Draw a line graph with the ring number along the bottom and the score up the side. Write one sentence about the shape of the line.
maths.answer: A line that starts high and slopes down. The jumps got smaller as the spoon was rung again and again.
maths.explain: A falling line shows getting used to the sound. If the line jumps up at the new sound, it shows the person was not simply tired.
maths.context: In the Spoon Test, you scored each jump of your volunteers on a scale of 0, 1 or 2.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows a change over time at a glance, and shows the shape of getting used to a sound.

maths.problem: A sea slug has about 20,000 nerve cells. A human brain has about 86 billion. About how many times more nerve cells does a human brain have? Round the answer.
maths.answer: About 4,300,000 times as many, or about four million.
maths.explain: 86,000,000,000 divided by 20,000 is 4,300,000. So a human brain has more than four million times as many nerve cells. Yet the slug shows the same kind of change at one connection.
maths.context: In this unit you learned that a sea slug with a very small nervous system can still show a simple kind of learning.
maths.why_maths: Comparing big numbers shows how small the slug's nervous system is, and why it was easier to trace one pathway there.

maths.problem: You study the spread-out list at 8:00 am, and then again every 90 minutes. Write the times of the four sittings. How long is it from the first to the last?
maths.answer: 8:00 am, 9:30 am, 11:00 am and 12:30 pm. It is 4 hours and 30 minutes.
maths.explain: 8:00 plus 90 minutes is 9:30. 9:30 plus 90 minutes is 11:00. 11:00 plus 90 minutes is 12:30. From 8:00 to 12:30 is 4 hours and 30 minutes.
maths.context: In Crammed or Spread Out, one list is studied in four short sittings spread through the day.
maths.why_maths: A plan with clear times makes sure the breaks between sittings are long enough to count as spaced practice.

roots.context: In the Spoon Test, we tested whether a person gets used to a sound. We also looked at learning in sea slugs, bees and meerkats. Now we ask what getting used to something tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: When the same harmless thing keeps happening, even a one-celled pond animal can stop reacting to that thing. That is not carelessness. It is the simplest kind of learning, because the body keeps the change. So learning begins with finding out what does not matter.
deep_truth.habit: We think learning means adding something new, and that ignoring means not paying attention. But getting used to a harmless sound is a change that is kept, and it is specific to that sound. It is learning too.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Spoon Test, the jumps got smaller with each ring of the spoon, yet a new sound brought the jump back at once. Sea slugs, one-celled swimmers and slime moulds all show the same pattern.

three.who_am_i: All day you ignore your clothes, the fan and the fridge. Your body has learned to leave them out, and that learning is part of who you are.
three.what_is_life: A sea slug, a one-celled swimmer and a slime mould all get used to harmless things. So a change like learning is older than brains. Living things could do this before any of them had a brain.
three.what_is_this_world: The world sends signals all the time. Every living being sorts them into the ones that matter and the ones that do not.

roots.thread: A sea slug touched again and again sends less chemical across one connection. A one-celled swimmer and a slime mould change in a similar way, with no nerve cells at all. In each case, something happens to a living being, the being changes, and the change is kept. That is what learning is. The change can be as small as one connection between two nerve cells, or as large as a whole way of living, such as a bee knowing the time of day.

teachings.teaching: Practice becomes firmly rooted when it is kept up for a long time, without a break, and with care.
teachings.link: Spread-out practice lasted longer than cramming in the sea slug and, perhaps, in your own lists of words in Crammed or Spread Out.

teachings.link: Getting used to something makes a being calm and quick, but she stops noticing it. A new sound makes her notice again. A beginner notices what an expert has stopped seeing.

science.text: After many gentle touches, a sea slug's touch-sensing cell sends less chemical across its connection to the next cell. Eric Kandel's team showed in the 1970s that learning changes the connection between nerve cells.
Whether one-celled animals, slime moulds and plants learn in the same sense as animals with nerves is still argued about.

other_view.view: Some scientists say the word learning should be kept for animals with nervous systems. In a one-celled swimmer or a slime mould, they say, the change may be the cell's chemistry simply adjusting, and calling it learning stretches the word too far.

In my head it takes about 36 minutes. The jumps are scored by eye, so the scores are rough and two scorers may differ. how_we_found_out.story: For years, scientists thought that learning was too tangled to follow. From the 1920s, Karl Lashley trained rats to run a maze and then cut away parts of their brains, looking for the place where the memory lived. He never found one spot. Many people decided a memory was spread everywhere, and could not be traced to particular cells. In the 1960s, Eric Kandel chose a very different animal, the sea slug Aplysia. Their nerve cells are large enough to see, and the whole nervous system has only about 20,000 of them. When the slug's siphon (a small spout on its body) was touched gently again and again, the gill pulled in less each time. Kandel and his team followed the message through the cells. They found that the cell sensing the touch sent less chemical across its connection to the next cell. A simple memory could be traced to a single connection. Kandel shared a Nobel Prize for this work in 2000.
how_we_found_out.who: Karl Lashley, and then Eric Kandel and his team at New York University
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That learning was too spread out through a brain to be traced to particular cells and connections.

quiz: A sparrow that stops fleeing a scarecrow has learned that the scarecrow does no harm.
Getting used to something harmless that keeps happening is a kind of learning.
If an animal stops reacting to a sound, she must simply be tired.
Tiredness would slow reactions to everything. Getting used to something belongs to that one sound.
A bee learns only the colour of a flower that pays.
Bees also learn the smell, shape, place and even the time of day.
A new sound can bring back a reaction that had grown weak.
The weakening belongs to the old sound only, so a new sound starts the reaction again.
An animal can learn to avoid a food after being ill only once.
Linking a taste to feeling ill can happen in one go, because it is so important to stay safe.
Learning changes nothing in the nerve cells, only in what the animal does.
Learning changes how strongly the gaps between nerve cells pass their messages.
Young songbirds sing the right song without ever hearing adults.
Many young songbirds need to hear adults of their own kind during an early window.
Practice spread over several days usually lasts longer than practice crammed into one sitting.
Breaks between sittings help the change in the brain to last.
An animal is teaching whenever a young one simply watches what she does.
Teaching needs her to change what she does for the learner, at a cost, so the learner learns faster.
A strong scare can make an animal react more strongly to many things afterwards.
This rise in alertness is called sensitisation, and it is the opposite of getting used to things.
odd: You stop hearing a fridge hum
The first three are getting used to harmless things that keep happening. Thunder for the first time is new and strong.
The first three are learned links between two things. A knee jerk is a reflex, ready at birth.
The first three spread practice over time, which lasts longer. Cramming squeezes it into one sitting.
A bang, a smell and a touch are things sensed, called stimuli. Running away is what a being does in response.
The first three are a rise in reaction after a strong event. Ignoring a harmless hum is a drop.
